Learning Objectives
Distinguish between billing and coding.
Assess the purpose and goals of billing and coding systems.
Explain the components and function of the resource-based relative value scale system.
Delineate between the types of codes and how they are used.
Determine the code for an office visit and a surgical procedure.
Introduction
Billing and coding allow for accurate communication of the services offered by a physician and
the value of those services.


Introduction
Billing and coding refers to the processes and systems that allow for clear
communication of a physician’s services and accurate valuing of those services. Billing
and coding are the two translational steps that occur in this process. Coding describes
the first step in translation, in which the patient visit is converted into specific numeric or
alphanumeric code. The second translational step is billing, in which the codes are used
to generate the total value of the service provided. In basic terms, coding can be
considered a universal language used to communicate the specific services provided
among healthcare providers, insurance companies, and government agencies.
Conversely, billing determines the value of the services and uses coding language to
correspond with insurance providers to determine the amount insurance covers and the
amount the patient owes.
Coding
Coding is the process that translates services offered by a physician into an alphanumeric
code. 

Coding
Coding is the process that translates a physician’s or healthcare provider’s service into a
numeric or alphanumeric value. For example, an orthopedic surgeon who performed a
total knee arthroplasty procedure must clarify what exactly was done before the service
can be billed. Did the procedure involve the medial compartment, the lateral
compartment, or both compartments? Was it a revision procedure? These variables can
be condensed into distinct codes that correlate with the specific procedure. This
minimizes confusion and ensures all healthcare providers are properly reimbursed for
their services.
Physicians must be able to navigate the coding language and document their services in
ways that are reflective of the coding language. For example, for a particular code to

apply to a service, the documentation must contain specific language. If the provider fails
to include this language in his or her documentation, the claim likely will be delayed or
denied.
Billing
Billing translates alphanumeric codes into dollar values for reimbursement. 

Billing
Billing is the process of interpreting the patient visit codes, determining the cost of the
services provided, and coordinating the payment between the insurance company and
the patient. The codes from a particular visit are compiled into a claim, which is
submitted to the patient’s insurance company and reviewed. The billing office then
determines the final cost to the patient after subtracting the insurance company’s
contribution.
Types of Codes
Two main categories of codes exist: diagnostic codes and procedural. 
Diagnostic codes refer to international classification of disease (ICD) codes.
Procedural codes refer to current procedural terminology (CPT) codes.
Procedural codes can be divided into evaluation and management and surgical coding.
Evaluation and management coding typically refer to office-based coding. 

Types of Code
Codes can be divided into two categories: diagnostic codes and procedural codes.
Diagnostic codes describe pathologic or disease states. They are known as ICD codes.

Procedural codes describe provider services and are known as CPT codes. Typically,
these codes are paired in generating a bill to justify the need for the services provided.
ICD Codes

ICD Codes
ICD-10 is the most current iteration of the ICD codex and went into effect in October
2015. In this most current version, a particular disease or pathology is described using a
seven-digit alphanumeric value. Consider a physician who is seeing a patient for a follow-
up visit regarding an open (type II), displaced, comminuted femoral shaft fracture of the
right leg. Radiographs are obtained and demonstrate routine healing with no evidence of
nonunion. This encounter correlates with ICD code S72.351E. The first three digits, S72,
indicate the category of the disease, a femur fracture. The subsequent two digits
describe subcategories of the broader pathology.
In this example, S72.3 describes a femoral shaft fracture, whereas S72.35 describes a
comminuted femoral shaft fracture. The last two digits add further descriptions to the
disease and the nature of the visit. In this case, the sixth digit describes whether the
fracture was on the right, left, or unspecified side of the body. The code S72.351
indicates the fracture affects the right femur, and S72.352 indicates the left femur is
involved. Finally, the seventh digit of the ICD code states the fracture classification
(closed or open type I, type II, type IIIA, type IIIB, type IIIC), the manner in which the
fracture is healing, and the patient encounter. If this were the initial visit and the fracture
was closed, the code would read S72.351A; however, this is a follow-up visit and the
fracture is healing well, the ICD code reads S72.351E.
CPT Codes

CPT Codes
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:28 AM
AAOS | Billing and Coding
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001022
4/14

CPT codes identify specific procedures, services, or treatment options provided to the
patient and typically consist of a five-digit number or letter/number combination. They
often are associated with a billing value. For an orthopedic practice, two main categories
of CPT coding are applicable: evaluation and management coding and surgical coding.
Evaluation and Management Coding
Evaluation and management coding underwent a major update in January of 2021.
Evaluation and management coding is based on three principles: a medically appropriate
patient history and physcial examination, medical decision making (MDM), and time spent with
the patient. 

Evaluation and Management Coding
Evaluation and management coding was updated on January 1, 2021. The following
information summarizes the new updates. The CPT codes that describe physician-
patient encounters are referred to as evaluation and management codes. Various
evaluation and management codes are available for different types of encounters, such
as office visits or hospital visits. Distinct levels of care are described within each type of
encounter. Typically, five levels of care, escalating in complexity, exist. For example, the
99214 code may be used to charge for an office visit with an established patient. The
99214 code often is called a level 4 office visit because the code ends in 4. Therefore,
each patient care encounter may be viewed as a unique procedure that requires specific
documentation.
The following is a basic template that can be used to apply evaluation and management
coding to patient visits. The first consideration is patient type. For purposes of billing for
evaluation and management services, patients are identified as new or established,
depending on previous encounters with the provider.
New patient: An individual who did not receive any professional services within the
previous 3 years from the physician/nonphysician practitioner or another physician of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:28 AM
AAOS | Billing and Coding
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001022
5/14

the same specialty who belongs to the same group practice.
Established patient: An individual who received professional services within the
previous 3 years from the physician/nonphysician practitioner or another physician of
the same specialty who belongs to the same group practice.
Next, the three key components in selecting the appropriate level of evaluation and
management services provided are a medically appropriate patient history and physical
examination, MDM, and time spent with the patient. The 2021 updates to evaluation and
management coding allow the provider to determine the appropriate level of patient
history and physical examination. Medically appropriate means that the physician or
other qualified healthcare professional reporting the evaluation and management
determines the nature and extent of any patient history or physical examination for a
particular service. Specific requirements no longer are required to reach a designated
level of coding. Therefore, the guidelines do not quantify these elements.
MDM is the most notable change in the 2021 update. The appropriate level of evaluation
and management coding is based on multiple factors. These factors can be viewed and
coding determined by accessing the CPT Evaluation and Management Office Revisions
Level of Medical Decision Making chart (Resource 1). To summarize these decision-
making variables, the 2021 MDM chart has three main columns, with the final column
divided into three additional columns:
Code
Level of MDM (Based on 2 out of 3 Elements of MDM)
Elements of Medical Decision Making
Number and Complexity of Problems Addressed
Amount and/or Complexity of Data to be Reviewed and Analyzed
Risk of Complications and/or Morbidity or Mortality of Patient Management
Use of these variables and the chart allows for appropriate coding.
Also new in the 2021 updates is codes used to define time spent during the visit. Time
alone may be used to select the correct code from 99202 to 99205 and 99212 to 99215.

separately; performing the physical examination; counseling and providing education to
the patient, family, or caregiver; ordering medicines, tests, or procedures;
communicating with other healthcare professionals; documenting information in the
medical record; interpreting results and sharing that information with the patient, family,
or caregiver; and care coordination.

Overall, evaluation and management coding of new and established office visits has
become more straightforward with the 2021 updates. Understanding these components
is essential to apply appropriate coding and allow for appropriate billing.
Surgical CPT Codes
CPT coding is used to translate a surgical report or other procedure into a code thta can be
used for billing.

Physicians must have a detailed surgical report and understand CPT coding that applies to
procedures completed. 

Surgical CPT Codes
Each surgical procedure can be recognized with a CPT code. Specific procedures have a
correlating CPT code, whereas other procedures that do not have a specific CPT code are
classified as unlisted, with an unlisted CPT code assigned. Multiple CPT codes can be
assigned to each surgical procedure based on the procedures performed. Typically, each
successive CPT code will have a discount applied to it during conversion into billing and
reimbursement for a surgical procedure. Therefore, surgeons must understand the
value of CPT codes and the subsequent order for submitting to billing.
The following are tips for documentation in a surgical report. Many of these tips have
been adapted from the teachings of and articles by Karen Zupko and Associates and
provide an excellent basis for creating surgical reports that can be successfully
translated into CPT coding and subsequently billing.
Preoperative and Postoperative Diagnoses

Preoperative and Postoperative Diagnoses
All relevant preoperative and postoperative diagnoses should be documented, including
underlying comorbid conditions considered relevant for the procedure performed. A
preoperative diagnosis that is no longer relevant or changes intraoperatively should be
documented in the postoperative diagnosis statement.
Procedures Performed

Procedures Performed
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:28 AM
AAOS | Billing and Coding
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001022
8/14

The procedures performed are listed in this area of the surgical note, which typically is
on the top half of the first page. The author of this lesson recommends using CPT
terminology as much as possible but not including codes in the surgical note. The reason
is that the codes documented in the surgical note often are not accurate.
A compliance issue arises if the codes in the surgical report do not match the codes
billed on the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) 1500 claim form.
Indications for Surgical Management

Indications for Surgical Management
This short paragraph, a couple of sentences, is especially important because it provides
the clinical necessity for the procedure being performed. Any previous, related surgical
procedures on the same or different structure/wound should be documented. The
reason the patient is being brought back to the operating room should be noted.
Whether future surgery is planned should be reported. This information serves as clues
for coders to support specific modifiers.
Complexity

Complexity
This separate paragraph is necessary if modifier 22 (increased procedural services) will
be used to obtain additional payment. This information should summarize the added
complexity that will be in the subsequent details documented in the surgical note. A
payor should not be expected to wade through the details of the surgical note to
determine whether a surgeon should receive additional reimbursement. Surgeons
should make it easy for the payor to feel the pain of the procedure in a complexity, or
findings at surgery, paragraph.

Details or Description of Procedure

Details or Description of Procedure
This section typically is the lengthiest area of the surgical note and describes the
procedures performed in great detail. The details in this section should support the
procedures listed in the aforementioned procedures performed section, which also
should support the CPT codes reported for the procedure. An understanding of the
requirements of the CPT codes that have been defined for the procedure is essential to
ensure all elements are met in the surgical report.
Updating CPT Codes

Updating CPT Codes
Any healthcare professional can submit an application to add, change, or delete an
existing CPT code. These applications are reviewed by the American Medical Association
CPT editorial board, a collection of 19 individuals comprising 11 representatives from
specialty societies, 6 representatives from payors and/or hospitals, and 2
representatives from the CPT healthcare professionals advisory committee. The editorial
board assesses the applications and determines whether to consider the request. If
further consideration is granted, the request is investigated by surveying the involved
societies to better determine support for such a change. The American Medical
Association’s Relative Value Scale Update Committee then ascertains any necessary
changes to the relative value scale value of the code before sending it to the CMS for
evaluation. If the CMS agrees with the proposed change, it will issue an updated
proposed rule followed by a subsequent open comment period to assess the effect of
the change before deciding to finalize the change.
Resource-Based Relative Value Scale

The resource based relative value scale assigns a value to the service codes of healthcare
providers in the form of relative value units (RVUs). 
RVUs are based on the resource expenditure of physician work, practice expense, and
professional liability insurance. 
An RVU is converted to a dollar amount to determine reimbursement rates. 
Resource-Based Relative Value Scale

Resource-Based Relative Value Scale
The resource-based relative value scale is a payment system adopted by the CMS and
most other payors for the reimbursement of healthcare services. This system assigns a
value to service codes of healthcare providers in the form of RVUs. RVUs are based on
the resource expenditure of the following components: physician work, practice
expense, and professional liability insurance. Physician work includes the provider’s
time, technical skill, effort, knowledge, and judgment. It also incorporates stress
associated with any patient risks that the service entails. Physician work accounts for
about 51% of the RVUs assigned to a service. Practice expense accounts for costs
associated with upkeep of the business, including wages, supply costs, and other bills. It
is calculated from an equation that analyzes mean Medicare charges and the proportion
of the revenue that goes to practice expense. Practice expense accounts for
approximately 45% of the RVU assigned to a service. The remaining 4% of the RVU is
derived from the professional liability insurance and considers expenses associated with
malpractice insurance.
After a service is assigned an RVU, the RVU is converted to a dollar amount to determine
reimbursement rates. The RVU is first adjusted to the geographic location according to
the geographic cost indices to account for differences in geographic costs. The new RVU
is then multiplied by the physician fee schedule conversion factor, which converts the
RVU to its final dollar amount. For example, CPT code 27447 represents total knee
arthroplasty and is assigned 39.07 RVUs. If the procedure was performed in Wisconsin,
where the geographic cost indices for physician work, practice expense, and professional
liability have conversion factors of 1.000, 0.949, and 0.322, respectively, the
geographically adjusted RVU is 37.11, assuming the breakdown of the total RVU adheres

to the approximate percentages of 51% physician work, 45% practice expense, and 4%

$36.0896, the final value associated with the code is $1,339.28.
The resource-based relative value scale is used by payors rather than healthcare
providers. The actual cost of a service to a healthcare system may be different than that
determined by the resource-based relative value scale.
In larger cases, an assistant surgeon or co-surgeon may work with the primary surgeon.
Understanding the manner in which to code these situations is critical. The surgical
notes should clearly identify the role of each surgeon primary surgeon, co-surgeon, and
assistant surgeon) and document the procedures performed.
The role of primary surgeon is self-explanatory. Distinct differences exist between a co-
surgeon and an assistant surgeon. A co-surgeon performs a separate part of the same
procedure. For example, a general surgeon performs an approach to the lumbar spine,
and then a spine surgeon performs a fusion. These providers are co-surgeons. For both
surgeons to receive appropriate reimbursement, they must not be assisting each other
but rather performing distinct and separate parts of the same procedure with separate
dictations. Both surgeons would then report their respective codes with a CPT code -62
modifier on the primary procedure. Subsequent procedures would be reported with the
assistant surgeon modifier if one of the surgeons remained involved and assisted on the
case.
If an assistant surgeon participates in a surgical procedure, the surgeon of record is
responsible for identifying the presence of the assistant surgeon. In this situation, the
assistant surgeon does not dictate a surgical note but assists in the procedures
performed. Two possible modifiers can be applied: modifier 80 for an assistant surgeon
who assisted on most of the case or modifier 81 for an assistant surgeon who assisted
on less than most of the case. Typically, an assistant surgeon is reimbursed at 16% of the
allowable charges, and in co-surgery, surgeons are reimbursed at 63% of the allowable
charges.

Summary

Summary
Understanding billing and coding in the orthopedic space is essential to ensure proper
reimbursement and medicolegal protection from mis-coding or mis-billing. ICD-10
diagnosis codes provide a diagnosis for each encounter that carries through to establish
appropriate procedural coding. Procedural coding involves the application of CPT codes
to a patient-physician clinical or surgical interaction. Evaluation and management coding
requires the appropriate clinical documentation to support a level of the physician-
patient clinical interaction. Lastly, RVUs are an established metric to determine the work
requirements for a given procedure or interaction. The units can then be applied to
determine specific reimbursement levels.
Coding typically is not a component of orthopedic training programs and often is left to
the coders; however, an understanding of the fundamentals of billing and coding is
critical to the success of an upstart orthopedic practice via the increase in
reimbursement, decrease in denials, and medicolegal protection of appropriate
documentation.
